junction.name: Woodhaven Boulevard & Jamaica Avenue, New York City

claims.text: Woodhaven Boulevard & Jamaica Avenue had 53 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 12 pedestrians injured, 5 cyclists injured and 1 person killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $3.6 million a year.
18% of crashes here had “failure to yield right-of-way” recorded as a contributing factor, against 8% at the city's priority junctions.
12% of crashes here had “traffic control disregarded” recorded as a contributing factor, against 3% at the city's priority junctions.

Held up on later years: a vehicle was going straight ahead, heading north and it happened in the daytime in 26% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 11% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search).

Held up on later years: a vehicle was going straight ahead, heading north and only people in vehicles hurt in 20% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 6% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search and the exhaustive search).

This corner got turn traffic calming in 2018. Across the city: a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program. Repeating it here is not supported by the city's own record.

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: worked (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).
Yellow Change Intervals would avoid about 2.9 crashes a year (CMF 4215, the median of 4 eligible records), worth $987,000 a year.
Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 1.6 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites), worth $544,000 a year.
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for Woodhaven Boulevard, Jamaica Avenue (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 32, New York City Council; Queens Community Board 9.
A request letter to the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is ready to draft from these facts.
